analysis.one_liner: Strengthens penalties for employers who don't pay workers their full wages.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have raised damages and penalties for wage theft, was introduced in July 2017 and referred to the Senate labor committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill amends federal wage law to fight wage theft: employers not paying workers what they're owed. It would require employers to give new hires written terms of employment, regular paystubs, and final pay within 14 days of leaving a job. It would raise damages owed to workers from twice to three times the unpaid wages, stretch the deadline to sue from two years to four (five for willful violations), bar employers from forcing workers into arbitration instead of court over wage claims, and require criminal referral of repeat offenders who falsify records or retaliate. It would also fund $50 million a year in grants to community groups that help workers recover unpaid wages.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers who are shorted on pay: the bill's findings cite estimates that wage theft costs workers more than $15 billion a year, and that in some industries fewer than half of employers comply with wage laws. Women, immigrants, and Black workers are disproportionately affected, according to the bill's findings. Workers with a contract or union agreement promising more than minimum wage would gain a federal right to that higher rate. Workers who complain or cooperate with investigations would get triple damages if fired for it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers whose pay is shorted

how_it_helps.text: Every employer would have to give workers a written statement of their pay rate, classification, and how pay is calculated, plus itemized paystubs showing hours worked, overtime, and deductions.
Damages for wage theft would rise from twice the unpaid wages to three times, plus interest, and the deadline to sue would stretch from two years to four years (five for willful violations).
Workers could not be forced to sign away their right to sue in court over wages as a condition of employment or in a pre-dispute arbitration agreement.

Employers would have to pay a departing worker all unpaid wages within 14 days, and workers could request copies of their own wage records going back five years; if an employer's records are missing or incomplete, the worker's own evidence of unpaid hours would be presumed accurate unless the employer proves otherwise.

Employers who willfully falsify wage records, commit wage violations, and retaliate against workers would be referred to the Department of Justice for criminal prosecution, and civil fines would rise to $2,000 per affected employee per initial violation and $10,000 for repeat or willful violations.

The Department of Labor would run a $50 million-a-year grant program for community groups, unions, and legal aid organizations that educate workers about their rights and help them recover unpaid wages.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially those in low-wage industries with high rates of wage violations, would bear the cost: higher damages and fines, new recordkeeping and paystub obligations, faster final-pay deadlines, and litigation exposure in court rather than arbitration. Law-abiding employers would gain a more level playing field against competitors who cut costs by not paying workers fully.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall hardest on small businesses: the bill requires new disclosures at hire, itemized paystubs with many required data points, and a final-pay deadline of 14 days or the end of the pay period, whichever comes first.

The bill raises the stakes of wage lawsuits considerably: triple damages, a longer statute of limitations, and a rule that a worker's own account of hours worked is presumed accurate if the employer's records are incomplete could push more disputes into litigation and settlement even where violations are disputed.
The grant program would authorize $50 million a year in new federal spending through fiscal 2021, routed to unions and community nonprofits that would work with the Labor Department on enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the upside is direct: billions of dollars a year in wages that the bill's findings say go unpaid, concentrated among the lowest-paid workers. The costs fall on employers, particularly small ones, in the form of paperwork, faster final pay, and greater litigation risk, and on taxpayers for the grant program. The arbitration ban and presumption rules are the most aggressive parts and would predictably draw lawsuits from business groups. Weighing it honestly: the bill targets a documented, large-scale transfer of pay from the lowest earners to their employers, and its costs are the price of enforcement, though the multipliers and presumptions tilt the legal playing field heavily toward workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, so it died without a hearing, markup, or vote when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the bill on July 27, 2017, with 19 Senate colleagues listed on it, and it was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
Twenty-one senators cosponsored the bill, 20 Democrats and one Independent; no Republican signed on.
The committee took no further action: the bill's complete action history shows only the introduction and the committee referral, with no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action.
The bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, without ever coming to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay less than the full wages owed, and who would have faced higher damages, fines, criminal referral, and court access for workers, are better off because the bill never advanced. Law-abiding employers who compete against them also keep the status quo, which the bill's findings describe as a competitive disadvantage for following the rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who don't pay full wages

industries.industry: Low-wage service employers (restaurants, retail, home care, janitorial, agriculture)
industries.note: These industries have the highest rates of wage violations, and the bill would expose them to triple damages, higher fines, criminal referral for repeat offenders, and lawsuits in court rather than arbitration. Their interest in stopping the bill runs directly against the workers they underpay.

The bill's findings target networks of interconnected employers that shift wage liability, and its contract-wage and recordkeeping rules would make it harder to shift pay obligations onto workers or lower tiers of subcontractors.

industries.industry: Arbitration industry and employers using mandatory arbitration
industries.note: The bill bars employers from requiring workers to give up their right to sue over wages in pre-dispute arbitration agreements, removing a tool employers use to keep wage disputes out of class actions.

industries.industry: Labor unions and worker advocacy nonprofits
industries.note: They would be eligible for a share of $50 million a year in federal grants to educate workers and help them recover unpaid wages, and the bill would give unions a federal backstop to enforce collectively bargained wage rates.

The bill's own findings argue that wage theft puts law-abiding employers at a competitive disadvantage; they would face the same paperwork and paystub rules but would benefit from enforcement against underpaying competitors.
